content.text: In everyday language, "work" means any kind of effort or activity. In physics, work has a very specific meaning — it is done when a force causes an object to move. No movement, no work (in the physics sense). A person holding a heavy box stationary is not doing any work on the box, even though they feel tired.

If an object does not move, no work is done, regardless of the force applied.

If the force is perpendicular to the direction of movement, no work is done by that force. For example, if you carry a box horizontally, the upward force you exert (supporting the box against gravity) does no work because it is perpendicular to the horizontal direction of movement. However, gravity does no work on the box either (in horizontal movement), so no energy is transferred to or from the gravitational store.

Example 8: Work from a Force-Distance Graph

Machine A lifts a 100 kg load through 5 m in 10 s. Machine B lifts a 200 kg load through 5 m in 25 s. Which machine is more powerful?
Machine A is more powerful (500 W > 400 W), even though Machine B does more total work.
A student carries a 30 N bag and walks 200 m along a horizontal corridor. How much work does the student do on the bag?
The force on the bag (upward) is perpendicular to the direction of movement (horizontal). Therefore:
No work is done on the bag. The student does work against friction in their muscles and joints, but they do not do work on the bag (its energy does not change).
"If you push hard, you must be doing work."
Work requires both force and movement in the direction of the force. Pushing against a solid wall does no work on the wall (the wall does not move).
"Carrying a heavy object is doing work on it."
Carrying a bag along a horizontal surface does no work on the bag because the force (upward) is perpendicular to the displacement (horizontal).
"Power tells you how much work is done."
Power tells you how quickly work is done, not the total amount. A machine with lower power can do more total work if it runs for a longer time.
"A more powerful machine always does more work."
A more powerful machine does work more quickly, but the total work depends on both power and time:
Work and energy are both measured in joules. Work done equals energy transferred.
The energy is not lost — it is transferred to thermal energy. The total energy is conserved, but the useful energy is reduced.
"The watt is a unit of energy."

The watt is a unit of power (energy per second). The unit of energy is the joule. A common confusion arises with electricity — a "100 watt" light bulb uses 100 joules per second, not 100 joules total.
